scenarios.name: Rat Tail Bounty
scenarios.gamingNarrative: Tail-collectors realize killing wild rats is slow and dangerous. Breeding rats in backyard farms is faster — and the bounty office can't tell a farmed tail from a wild one.

historical.headline: What actually happened in Hanoi
facts: French colonial administrators paid a bounty for every rat tail turned in.
Hunters started cutting off tails and releasing the rats alive to breed more tails.
Some residents began farming rats specifically to harvest tails for cash.
The wild rat population kept climbing even as tail payouts hit historic highs.

scenarios.name: Cross-Sell Quota
scenarios.gamingNarrative: Branch staff facing an "8-accounts-a-day" quota start opening extra checking and credit accounts in existing customers' names — without telling them.

historical.headline: What actually happened at the bank
facts: A nationwide cross-sell quota pushed staff to open as many new accounts as possible per customer.
Employees opened an estimated 3.5 million accounts customers never asked for.
Many customers were charged fees on accounts they didn't know existed.
The bank paid over $3 billion in fines and settlements once regulators uncovered the practice.

scenarios.name: Ticket Quota Precinct
scenarios.setting: A generalized pattern seen in traffic-enforcement units
scenarios.gamingNarrative: To hit a ticket count, officers start writing citations for trivial, easy-to-prove infractions near the station instead of patrolling the actual high-risk stretches of road.

historical.headline: A widely documented pattern, not one specific case
facts: This scenario is a generalized pattern described in criminology and public-administration research on quota policing, not a single real agency.
Researchers have repeatedly found that raw ticket-count quotas can shift effort toward easy, low-value stops.
The result: citation counts look great on a dashboard while the riskiest roads see little change in actual safety.
Several police departments have since moved to outcome-based metrics (crash rates, repeat offenders) instead of raw ticket counts.
